title: Mayor wants to see Stockport regeneration inspire other areas

input.summary: Mayor of Greater Manchester Bev Craig wants other areas to follow Stockport's lead
input.evidence_text: The mayor of Greater Manchester has said she hopes the £1bn regeneration of Stockport town centre can be replicated in towns across the region The Stockport Mayoral Development Corporation (MDC) was launched seven years ago and has ambitions to build 8,000 new homes in the town centre by 2040 Bev Craig, who became metro mayor of Greater Manchester in July, said: "I want to carry on and go further with the work of Mayoral Development Corporations across the region "I want to build genuinely affordable homes on publicly owned land and, by getting the private sector to back us, I'm excited about what we can achieve with our MDCs, in places like Ashton-under-Lyne, Stalybridge and Oldham." Mayoral Development Corporations are used to speed up regeneration projects by bringing land, funding, and planning powers together to attract investment They are able to use compulsory purchase powers to make sites available for housing projects and many MDCs are able to grant planning permission for developments

title: Manchester mayor calls for warehouse planning changes

input.lead: Bev Craig says planning rules should be reviewed after complaints about warehouses built near housing
input.summary: Bev Craig says planning rules should be reviewed after complaints about warehouses built near housing
input.evidence_text: Manchester mayor calls for warehouse planning changes - BBC News Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Residents on the Henfold Estate have raised concerns about warehouses being built at the nearby Astley Business Park By James Fell North West Published 13 August 2026 The mayor of Greater Manchester has said planning rules should be reviewed after complaints about warehouses being built close to people's homes. Speaking on BBC Radio Manchester's Hot Seat, Bev Craig said she agreed with concerns raised by campaigners from the Astley Warehouse Action Group and questioned why modern industrial developments were being allowed closer to residential properties than traditional industry. The group was formed after the construction of large warehouses at Astley Business Park near Tyldesley. Residents have complained about the scale of the development, its proximity to homes and concerns over noise from future operations. During Thursday's programme, campaigner John asked whether residents could continue to rely on mayoral support as they were entering what he described as a new phase of the campaign, focused on the effect the warehouses would have once fully operational. Craig said that lessons needed to be learned from the situation. "I think we have to go and look at proper planning rules around this as well, because old industry wouldn't have got that close to your house," she said. "So why is it that new industry can?" The mayor said she wanted to explore whether planning rules should be changed, and offered to meet residents to discuss their concerns. She added: "Other people can't be in the same situation in the future, and we need to look at what we can do to help you now." title: Worker fears 'no work-life balance' under BT relocation plan

input.lead: Lesley Wood says her commute to a new Manchester office would mean travelling for hours a day, as dozens hold a protest
input.summary: Lesley Wood says her commute to a new Manchester office would mean travelling for hours a day, as dozens hold a protest
input.evidence_text: Worker fears 'no work-life balance' under BT relocation plan - BBC News Image caption, Lesley Wood has worked for BT for 39 years and feels she has "no choice" but to relocate to Manchester By Thomas Berrington Reporting from Liverpool Published 13 August 2026 A British Telecom (BT) worker has described the planned closure of the Liverpool office and relocation of about 600 jobs as "absolutely horrendous", as dozens of workers held a protest. BT is due to close its Old Hall Street office in March when its lease runs out. The firm has said part of the reason is due to a hike in lease renewal costs. Roles will be moved to Manchester and Leeds and staff are being offered a chance to relocate but unions say it is not an option for many. Lesley Wood is being moved to the Manchester office and said she would have "no work-life balance" travelling three to four hours a day to and from her home in Southport. BT said it was taking concerns raised seriously. The telecom firm said the changes were part of an "optimisation and modernisation" of its working spaces. Wood has worked for BT for 39 years and been based at the Liverpool office since 2017. She told BBC Radio Merseyside the closure would have a big impact on her life. "It means I have to get up at 5.30am every morning. I'll have to get a train that takes one hour, 15 minutes. "I'm too close to retirement to get another job, so I've got no choice but to go there. "I'm just literally going to be coming home and going to bed." She said it was not the first time she had been relocated. "They did it to us in Warrington when they closed down BT Business." However, the prospect of closing the whole site was "absolutely horrendous" and would be a "really sad day" for all the staff there, she said. Image caption, Heather Taylor say

From the start of August through to the end of the month, highways crews will be out in force, carrying out surface dressing at nearly 30 locations across the city. Surface dressing is a cost-effective treatment that helps protect roads from everyday wear and tear. By sealing the road surface, it prevents water from entering small cracks and causing further deterioration. With the majority damage cause to the road surface during the winter months, work like this is vital to ensure the health of our road network, extending the life of our roads and reduce the need for more disruptive repairs in the future. Over the course of just two weeks, highways crews will treat approximately 154,000 square metres of road surface, covering more than 21 kilometres of carriageway across Manchester, roughly the distance from Manchester city centre to Glossop. The programme also incorporates the use of recycled granite chippings as part of Manchester City Council's commitment to more sustainable highway maintenance. title: Oldham bucks national trend as more young people choose education and training

input.evidence_text: Experience the raw, unfiltered power of Balkan folklore in a new immersive show from the world’s most famous performance artist Balkan Erotic Epic is a bold new performance work created by the iconic artist Marina Abramović . Regarded as the world’s most influential performance artist, Abramović’s transformative work has reached millions of people – from opening the Pyramid Stage at Glastonbury Festival t A four-hour ritual where ancient myth meets performance art, Balkan Erotic Epic explores the eroticism, spirituality and traditions of Abramović’s homeland through 13 visceral scenes Brought to life by a cast of over 70 performers, dancers, musicians and singers, the experience unfolds across Aviva Studios. Audiences are free to choose their own path – with pop-up encounters punctuating the action, bringing bodies together in dance, song and ritual Watch Fertility Rite , a fevered ritual where bodies writhe against the ground in a desperate call for fertility. Witness Massaging the Breast where women gesticulate over graves to awaken the earth. In Scaring the Gods , women bare themselves to the sky to banish storms. Listen Unafraid to push the boundaries of eroticism and performance art, Balkan Erotic Epic asks its audience a timeless question: What are our bodies truly for?

input.evidence_text: $7m funding round as Manchester startup addresses cyber risk of growing AI role in software development - Prolific North Skip to content Audio Veteran broadcaster John MacKay returns News MoneySuperMarket launches business bank with fintech partners News Former Sage software boss joins Newcastle clean tech scale-up $7m funding round as Manchester startup addresses cyber risk of growing AI role in software development Tech by Chris Newbould August 12, 2026 Manchester cybersecurity start-up Cytix has announced a $7M (£5m) Series A funding round to accelerate the company’s mission to tackle the problems created by rapid software change – a reality that is becoming a distinct risk for organisations as AI-assisted development, agentic workflows, and continuous delivery lead to an increased volume of AI-generated code. The round has been led by Northern Gritstone , the venture capital and investment firm that focuses on science and tech startups in the North of England, with participation from existing investors, Auriga Cyber Ventures and NPIF II – PXN Equity Finance, which is managed by PXN Ventures as part of the Northern Powerhouse Investment Fund II (NPIF II). Ben Armstrong, CEO of Cytix said: “We chose Northern Gritstone for their conviction in investing in deeptech companies in the North of England with global ambition. Northern Gritstone and Cytix share the belief that software change is becoming a key risk for organisations, and those that build software need a solution that scales with the current pace of development.
